description: How the Bank of England uses interest rates and the money supply to control inflation and influence demand.
content_html:
What Is Monetary Policy?

Monetary policy is operated by the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which is independent of the government. The government (HM Treasury and the Chancellor) sets the inflation target — 2% CPI — but the decision on interest rates is made solely by the MPC, not by politicians. In the United Kingdom, it is therefore the Bank of England that carries out monetary policy, not the government. The Bank does not aim simply to make profit — its primary job is to keep inflation low and stable so that households and firms can plan with confidence.

The key instrument of monetary policy is the bank rate, sometimes called the base rate or official bank rate. Commercial banks — such as high street lenders — borrow money from the Bank of England at this rate. Because their own costs depend on it, they pass the change on to their customers: when the bank rate rises, mortgage rates and loan rates go up across the whole economy. When it falls, they fall too.

Key Fact

The Bank of England's inflation target is 2% per year, measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI). The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets eight times a year and votes to raise, lower or hold the bank rate to keep inflation close to this target.

The Monetary Policy Committee

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is made up of nine members — including the Governor of the Bank of England — who vote on where to set the bank rate. The MPC is independent of the government, which means politicians cannot order it to cut rates before an election. This independence is designed to prevent short-term political pressures from causing long-term inflation damage.

When the MPC meets, it looks at data on inflation, economic growth, unemployment, and consumer confidence. If inflation is rising above 2%, the MPC will typically vote to raise the bank rate to cool spending. If the economy is in recession and inflation is falling below target, it is likely to cut the rate to encourage borrowing and spending.

How Changing Interest Rates Affects the Economy

A rise in the bank rate sets off a clear chain of effects. Think of it like turning down a tap on spending:

  • Mortgages and loans cost more. A homeowner on a variable-rate mortgage immediately pays more each month. This reduces their disposable income and they cut back on other spending — perhaps eating out less or delaying a new car.
  • Saving becomes more attractive. A higher bank rate means savings accounts pay more interest. Households may choose to save rather than spend, reducing demand across the economy.
  • Business investment falls. Firms that borrow to expand — to buy a new delivery fleet or open a second factory — face higher repayments. Some projects that looked profitable at 3% interest are no longer worthwhile at 6%. Investment spending falls, which slows economic growth.
  • Consumer credit becomes more expensive. Credit card rates and personal loan rates rise. Consumers buy fewer goods on credit, reducing demand.

The full transmission from a rate change to lower inflation typically takes one to two years. This time lag means the MPC must make forward-looking decisions based on forecasts, not just current data.

Key Fact

Bank rate rises → borrowing costs more → households and firms spend and invest less → demand in the economy falls → upward pressure on prices eases → inflation falls towards the 2% target.

Contractionary monetary policy means raising the bank rate. The aim is to reduce spending, cool inflation and prevent the economy from overheating. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more rewarding, which squeezes consumer demand. Firms invest less. The housing market may slow. The risk is that if rates go too high, unemployment rises and the economy tips into recession.

Expansionary monetary policy means cutting the bank rate. This is used when the economy is growing too slowly or is in recession. Lower rates make mortgages and loans cheaper, encouraging households to borrow and spend. Firms find investment more attractive because the cost of finance falls. Demand picks up, output rises and unemployment should fall. The risk is that if rates stay too low for too long, inflation can rise above target.

A useful way to remember the direction: HIRE to FIRE inflation — Higher Interest Rates Eliminate inflation. LIRE to HIRE growth — Lower Interest Rates Encourage growth.

Quantitative Easing

Quantitative easing (QE) is used when the bank rate has been cut as low as it can practically go — close to zero — but the economy still needs a boost. The Bank of England creates new money electronically and uses it to buy assets, mainly government bonds, from banks and other financial institutions. This injects money directly into the financial system.

With more money available and bond prices higher, interest rates on longer-term borrowing also fall. Banks are better capitalised and more willing to lend to businesses and households. The intention is to increase the flow of credit in the economy, supporting spending and investment. QE was first deployed by the Bank of England in March 2009, following the financial crisis that had intensified in 2007–08, and was used again on a large scale during the pandemic in 2020.

Monetary policy is controlled by the Bank of England’s MPC. Its main tools are the bank rate and quantitative easing. It works through the cost of borrowing and the supply of money. Changes act with a time lag of around one to two years.

Fiscal policy is controlled by the government (HM Treasury and the Chancellor of the Exchequer). Its main tools are taxation and government spending. Changes can act more quickly because government spending directly injects money into the economy, while tax cuts immediately raise household disposable income.

The key distinction: the Bank of England sets interest rates; the government sets taxes and spending. Both aim to achieve the same objectives — stable prices, low unemployment and steady economic growth — but use different levers. In practice, they must work in the same direction: expansionary fiscal policy alongside expansionary monetary policy will produce a stronger stimulus, but also a greater inflation risk.

The Limits of Monetary Policy

Monetary policy is a powerful tool, but it has limitations. First, it works with a time lag — a rate cut today will not lift consumer spending overnight. Second, if households and firms are already carrying high levels of debt, cutting rates further may not encourage more borrowing; people may simply feel too financially stretched. Third, a global economic shock — such as a sudden rise in oil prices — can push up inflation even when domestic interest rates are low. The Bank cannot control world commodity prices. Finally, QE risks increasing asset price inflation (property and shares become more expensive), which can widen inequality between those who own assets and those who do not.
exam_tip_html: When a question uses the command word Explain, you must build a chain of reasoning rather than just stating a fact. For monetary policy questions, the chain runs: bank rate changes → effect on borrowing costs → effect on household or business behaviour → effect on aggregate demand → effect on inflation or unemployment. Each arrow is worth marks. For Analyse questions, extend the chain and say how big or how certain the effect is. For Evaluate questions, you must discuss both sides — for example, raising rates reduces inflation but may also push up unemployment — and then make a supported judgement about which effect is stronger, using phrases such as “it depends on whether households are heavily indebted” or “in a recession, a rate cut may be less effective if confidence is already low.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Monetary policy is operated by the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, which sets the bank rate to keep inflation close to its 2% CPI target. Raising the rate cools inflation; cutting it stimulates spending and investment.
  • A rise in the bank rate increases the cost of borrowing for households and firms, reduces consumer spending and investment, and eases demand-pull inflation — but works with a one-to-two year time lag.
  • Quantitative easing is an additional tool used when the bank rate is already near zero: the Bank creates money electronically to buy assets, injecting funds into the financial system and lowering long-term interest rates.

practice_questions.text:
Which organisation is responsible for setting the bank rate in the United Kingdom?
A) HM Treasury
B) The Financial Conduct Authority
C) The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee
D) The Office for Budget Responsibility
practice_questions.marks: C) The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee. 1 mark for the correct answer.

practice_questions.text: A country's central bank cuts its bank rate from 5% to 4%. A household has a variable-rate mortgage with an outstanding balance of £200,000. Calculate the annual saving in interest payments for this household as a result of the rate cut. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Method: annual interest saving = change in rate × outstanding balance = 1% × £200,000. 1 mark for the correct method/formula; 1 mark for the correct answer of £2,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain why raising the bank rate might reduce consumer spending in the UK economy.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing (mortgages and loans become more expensive); 1 mark for explaining that households have less disposable income to spend; 1 mark for developing the chain — reduced consumer spending lowers aggregate demand in the economy.

practice_questions.text: A firm called Greenfield Logistics is planning to borrow £500,000 to buy new delivery vehicles. The bank rate has just been raised from 3% to 5.5%. Explain how this change in monetary policy is likely to affect Greenfield Logistics's investment decision.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that higher rates raise the cost of borrowing for the firm; 1 mark for explaining that the annual interest repayments on the loan will now be significantly higher; 1 mark for explaining that the investment may no longer be profitable or worthwhile at the higher rate; 1 mark for developing the consequence — Greenfield is likely to delay or abandon the investment, meaning productive capacity does not increase and potential job creation is lost.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a cut in the bank rate might help the government achieve its objective of reducing unemployment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained chain of reasoning linking the bank rate cut to lower unemployment, with analysis of the mechanism (lower borrowing costs → higher consumer spending and business investment → increased demand for labour → lower unemployment) and clear consideration of the scale and conditions under which the effect operates.
Secure: A clear causal chain linking the rate cut to reduced unemployment with developed explanation of at least two links in the chain.
Developing: Some correct points about lower interest rates boosting spending or investment, but the chain is incomplete or lacks development.
Emerging: Simple points about lower rates being good for the economy with limited or no connection to unemployment.

practice_questions.text:
'Raising the bank rate is always the most effective way for a government to control inflation.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Raising the bank rate increases the cost of borrowing, reducing household spending and business investment, which eases demand-pull inflation — this is the core transmission mechanism of monetary policy.
• The MPC is independent of political pressure, meaning rate decisions are based on economic data rather than electoral cycles, making the policy credible and predictable.
• Higher rates also make saving more attractive, further reducing consumer spending and cooling demand.
• Historical examples show that tight monetary policy can bring inflation down effectively when applied consistently.

Arguments against / limitations:
• Monetary policy acts with a significant time lag of one to two years, meaning rate rises may not reduce inflation quickly enough if it is rising rapidly.
• A rate rise is ineffective against cost-push inflation caused by global supply shocks (for example, a rise in global oil prices), because the Bank of England cannot control international commodity prices.
• Very high rates risk tipping the economy into recession, causing unemployment to rise — this conflicts with another government objective.
• If households and firms are already heavily indebted, a rate rise could trigger widespread defaults, destabilising the financial system rather than simply cooling demand.
• Fiscal policy tools (higher taxes or lower government spending) may also reduce inflation, offering an alternative approach.

Conclusion / Judgement:
• The strongest argument against the statement is the time lag and its inability to counter cost-push inflation — examiners reward a judgement such as: raising the bank rate is most effective when inflation is demand-driven and when the economy has time for the policy to work through; it is less effective in a supply-side crisis or when the economy is already fragile. It depends on the cause of inflation and the state of the wider economy.

Mastering: Sophisticated two-sided analysis with a clear supported judgement using 'it depends on' framing.
Secure: Both sides argued with some development and a stated conclusion.
Developing: Some arguments on both sides but limited development or a weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or largely descriptive response with little analytical chain.

The central bank cutting the bank rate to zero

Monetary policy in the UK is operated by the Bank of England's _____, which meets eight times a year to vote on the bank rate.
Match each monetary policy term to its correct description:
right: The interest rate set by the central bank that influences all other borrowing costs
Creating money electronically to buy assets and inject funds into the economy
Raising the bank rate to reduce spending and bring inflation down

flashcard_questions.a: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).

What is the Bank of England's inflation target?
flashcard_questions.a: 2% per year, measured by the Consumer Prices Index.

flashcard_questions.a: Cutting the bank rate to lower borrowing costs, stimulate spending and boost economic growth.
Raising the bank rate to increase borrowing costs and reduce spending to bring inflation down.
The central bank creates money electronically and buys financial assets to inject funds into the economy.

flashcard_questions.q: When is quantitative easing typically used?
flashcard_questions.a: When the bank rate is already near zero but the economy still needs a boost.

flashcard_questions.a: Around one to two years — monetary policy works with a significant time lag.

flashcard_questions.a: Because cost-push inflation comes from global supply shocks the Bank of England cannot control.

How does a rise in the bank rate affect a firm's decision to invest?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher borrowing costs make investment less profitable, so firms borrow and invest less.

glossary_terms.definition: The use of interest rates and the money supply by a central bank to influence inflation and economic activity.
The UK's central bank, responsible for setting the bank rate and maintaining price stability.
The interest rate set by the Bank of England that influences all other borrowing and saving rates across the economy.
A nine-member committee at the Bank of England that meets eight times a year to set the bank rate.

A form of expansionary monetary policy in which the central bank creates new money electronically and uses it to buy financial assets, such as government bonds, to increase money supply and encourage lending.
Raising the bank rate to increase the cost of borrowing, reduce consumer spending and investment, and bring inflation down towards its target.
Cutting the bank rate to reduce the cost of borrowing, stimulate consumer spending and business investment, and boost economic growth.
